results.title: The What, Why, and How of Mixture of Experts (MoE)
results.content:
1.   Experts. These are just small feed-forward networks, the same MLP block you already know from transformers. Nothing exotic. An “expert” is not a separate model, not a fine-tuned specialist, just one of several parallel MLPs living inside a layer.
2.   A router (or gating network). A tiny learned layer, often literally one linear layer — that looks at each token and produces a score for every expert. “This token? Expert 3 and Expert 7 look like the right fit.”
3.   Sparse activation. Instead of running all experts, we keep only the top-k scored ones (usually k=1 or k=2) and combine their outputs, weighted by the router’s confidence. The rest of the experts do nothing for that token. Zero FLOPs.

Here’s the part that surprises most people, so let’s deal with it now. [...] Serving is an infrastructure problem. At scale, experts get sharded across GPUs, so tokens must physically travel to their assigned experts and back every layer. Load balancing stops being just a training nicety and becomes a throughput requirement. This is why MoE inference is its own engineering subfield.
   Fine-tuning quirks. Sparse models historically overfit more easily during fine-tuning than dense ones, though modern recipes have largely tamed this. [...] return torch.einsum("be,bed->bd", weights, expert_outs)
This works, and it trains nicely. But notice: we ran _every_ expert on _every_ input. If we have 64 experts, that’s 64x the compute of a single FFN. We gained capacity but paid full price for it. This defeats the entire purpose.

[0:00] In deep learning, neural networks, including large language models, can be big. Very big. Like hundreds of billions of parameters big.
[0:08] And running them at inference time is usually a very compute intensive operation.
[0:14] So enter Mixture of Experts, which is a machine learning approach that divides an AI model into separate subnetworks, or "experts".
[0:24] Each expert focuses on a subset of the input data, and only the relevant experts are activated for a given task.
[0:31] Rather than using the entire network for every operation. Now, mixture of experts isn't new. Not at all.
[0:38] It goes back to a paper published in 1991, when researchers proposed an AI system with separate networks, each specializing in different training cases.

results.title: Mixture of Experts Explained
results.content:
This setup introduces some challenges. For example, although large batch sizes are usually better for performance, batch sizes in MOEs are effectively reduced as data flows through the active experts. For example, if our batched input consists of 10 tokens, five tokens might end in one expert, and the other five tokens might end in five different experts, leading to uneven batch sizes and underutilization. The Making MoEs go brrr section below will discuss other challenges and solutions.

How can we solve this? A learned gating network (G) decides which experts (E) to send a part of the input:
